questions.q: List the seven supporting figures Bergman explicitly names in the essay (including the interview section) and state the one specific contribution each made to his development.
questions.a: (1) Father and mother — the strict home he rebelled against instilled efficiency, punctuality and thrift, (2) Torsten Hammaren — taught him theatre craft through four years in Gothenburg, (3) Alf Sjoberg — directed Torment from Bergman's script and taught him much, (4) Lorens Marmstedt — taught him film-making from scratch and the rule of being a devil to yourself, (5) Herbert Grevenius — believed in him as a writer and nudged him toward drama, (6) Carl Anders Dymling — backed creative integrity over profit and gave him freedom, (7) Umberto Eco — the interview voice who regrets selling film rights. Omitting Eco misses the comparative dimension, and listing objects as figures confuses symbols with people.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why Bergman places the "Significant Persons" section immediately before the "Cathedral-building" metaphor. What logical bridge do these supporting characters build?
questions.a: (1) The bridge — the named supporting characters are the human proof of the cathedral metaphor, each a master builder or labourer in his cathedral, (2) The logic — by listing them first as named individuals with specific lessons, Bergman shows the anonymous collective he idealises is built from concrete, named relationships, (3) The link — his freedom came from Dymling and his craftsmanship from his parents and Marmstedt, gifts from others rather than solo achievements, which prepares the conclusion that art loses its creative drive when separated from collective service. A student who calls the placement chronological order misses the argumentative structure, and treating the essay as a memoir rather than a polemic about art versus ego is the core misconception.

questions.q: Apply the "cathedral-builder" test to **one** supporting figure: If that person were removed from Bergman's life, which specific "stone" (skill, value, opportunity) would be missing from his cathedral? Choose any figure except the parents.
questions.a: (1) The missing stone — rigorous self-critique, (2) The rule — Marmstedt's unbreakable rule that you must watch your own work coldly and be a devil to yourself in the screening room, (3) The connection — Bergman ties this to good craftsmanship and the pride of a good craftsman, the quality control that keeps the cathedral from collapsing into self-indulgence, (4) The absence — without Marmstedt he might have stayed a talented but undisciplined conjurer, unable to sustain the conscientious professional identity that lets him face producers. A vague answer like he taught him film-making fails to extract specific textual evidence, and inventing lessons not in the text shows hallucination instead of close reading.

questions.q: Analyze the **contrast** between Bergman's supporting figures (mentors, producer) and Umberto Eco's experience with the film adaptation of *The Name of the Rose*. How do their respective "supporting characters" (Dymling vs. the film director Jean-Jacques Annaud) represent opposing models of the artist-industry relationship?
questions.a: (1) Bergman's model — Dymling places faith in a creative artist's responsibility over profit and loss calculations, a trust-based relationship that protects uncompromising vision, (2) Eco's model — the film adaptation overwrites the reading experience, fixing faces and reducing the layered club sandwich of meaning to jambon or cheese, a transactional relationship that strips the author of interpretive authority, (3) The synthesis — Bergman's supporting characters enable authorship while Eco's apparatus usurps it, one building the cathedral with his masons, the other watching his cathedral become a tour guide's attraction. Saying Bergman had good producers and Eco bad ones reduces a structural contrast to luck, and missing the sandwich metaphor ignores Eco's literary argument about layered meaning.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "Bergman's portrayal of his mentors is hagiographic (uncritically admiring) and serves to mythologize his own rise." Defend or refute using textual evidence.
questions.a: (1) Stance — refute with nuance, because each mentor's contribution is framed as a specific technical lesson rather than vague inspiration, (2) The specifics — Hammaren taught theatre craft, Sjoberg provided the Torment opportunity, Marmstedt supplied a corrective rule implying Bergman needed correction, and Grevenius encouraged writing despite his trouble with script-writing, (3) The balance — his parents appear as antagonists, a world to revolt against, and he admits his freedom is fragile, ending the moment he loses it, (4) The tone — craftsman-like gratitude rather than worship, crediting a tradition, and the only mythologising is the cathedral metaphor applied to all artists. Agreeing with the claim confuses gratitude with hagiography and falls for surface tone without the professional specificity.

questions.q: Create a 100-word "missing mentor" paragraph written in Bergman's voice, describing a fictional sixth mentor who taught him **sound design**. Use the same sentence rhythm, vocabulary level, and "lesson + personal detail" structure as the original text.
questions.a: (1) The opening — an Among the people who have meant something transition that names a mentor and an institution, (2) The lesson — a specific, technical claim about sound, such as silence is not absence but a texture you sculpt, (3) The personal detail — a concrete anecdote like recording the wind in the pines for three nights until pine and birch could be told apart, (4) The habit — a lasting professional practice such as mixing the silence before the first line of dialogue, rendered in Bergman's balanced, semi-formal cadence. A poor answer offers generic praise with no technical specificity, no personal anecdote and a wrong modern tone, missing that style is a deliberate rhetorical choice.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: In a non-fiction ______ essay like Bergman's "Film-Making," supporting characters are the real-life individuals — parents, mentors, collaborators — whom the author explicitly names and describes as having shaped his artistic vision, professional discipline, and philosophical outlook.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are assembling a ______ about a famous director.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can identify each supporting figure in the text, cite specific textual evidence for their influence on Bergman, and analyze how the *group* of supporting characters collectively reinforces the essay's core themes of collaborative craftsmanship ("cathedral-building"), artistic integrity versus commercial pressure, and the.
